1	\section{Experimental Setup}
2	\label{sec:experimental-setup}
3	
4	\subsection{Models}
5	\label{sec:models}
6	
7	We conduct experiments on two 7B-parameter instruction-tuned models that share the Qwen2 backbone architecture (28 Transformer layers, 28 attention heads with 4-group GQA):
8	
9	\paragraph{DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B} serves as our primary evaluation target. This model was distilled from DeepSeek-R1 \cite{deepseek-r1} and produces explicit chain-of-thought traces delimited by \texttt{<think>}$\cdots$\texttt{</think>} tags, yielding sequences with pronounced phase structure---extended reasoning followed by a concise solution. The structured generation pattern makes it well-suited for studying how sparsity interacts with distinct reasoning phases.
10	
11	\paragraph{Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct} \cite{qwen2.5} provides a cross-model replication. Although it shares the same backbone family, its instruction tuning does not enforce explicit reasoning delimiters, producing a different distribution of attention sparsity across the generation trajectory. Replication on this model tests whether our findings generalize beyond distillation-induced phase structure.
12	
13	Both models are loaded in \texttt{bfloat16} precision with eager attention (i.e., without FlashAttention) to permit direct manipulation of attention weight matrices during sparsity intervention.\footnote{An earlier \texttt{float16} configuration produced sporadic NaN values in Layer~27 of DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, affecting ${\sim}$8\% of logit positions. Switching to \texttt{bfloat16} eliminated all NaN occurrences; we additionally apply NaN-guarded filtering as a safety net.}
14	
15	
16	\subsection{Dataset}
17	\label{sec:dataset}
18	
19	We evaluate on a 50-problem stratified subset of the MATH-500 benchmark \cite{math500}, sampling uniformly across problem categories (algebra, geometry, number theory, combinatorics, etc.) with a fixed seed for reproducibility. Mathematical reasoning tasks are a natural testbed for our study: they elicit long chain-of-thought sequences (up to 2048 tokens) in which the model alternates between exploratory reasoning and structured computation---phases that differ markedly in attention sparsity. Each problem is decoded greedily (\texttt{max\_new\_tokens}$=$2048) to eliminate sampling variance.
20	
21	
22	\subsection{Compound Sparsity Configuration}
23	\label{sec:sparsity-config}
24	
25	We apply \emph{symmetric} compound sparsity: for a given sparsity level $s$, we prune the same fraction $s$ of attention heads and evict the same fraction $s$ of KV cache entries. We evaluate four sparsity levels $s \in \{0.15, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30\}$, spanning from mild to aggressive compression.
26	
27	\paragraph{Sparsity conditions.} For each problem and each sparsity level, we compute perplexity under four conditions: (i)~\emph{dense}---no intervention; (ii)~\emph{attn-only}---head pruning without KV eviction; (iii)~\emph{kv-only}---KV eviction without head pruning; and (iv)~\emph{both}---simultaneous head pruning and KV eviction.
28	
29	\paragraph{Eviction strategies.} We compare two KV cache eviction strategies:
30	
31	\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
32	\item \textbf{Importance-based.} Each KV position receives a score equal to its cumulative attention weight summed over all query positions and heads. To correct for the inherent causal bias---earlier positions accumulate more attention simply because they are attended to by more queries---we apply position normalization:
33	\begin{equation}
34	\label{eq:importance}
35	    \alpha_j = \frac{\sum_{i,h} a_{i,h,j}}{\texttt{seq\_len} - j}, \quad j \in \{1, \dots, T\},
36	\end{equation}
37	where $a_{i,h,j}$ is the attention weight from query~$i$, head~$h$ to key~$j$, and the denominator counts the number of queries that can attend to position~$j$ under causal masking. Position~0 (BOS) is always retained. The $T \cdot s$ positions with the lowest normalized scores are evicted.
38	
39	During masked forward passes, we guard against numerical instability from the interaction of head masking and KV eviction: zeroed-out heads that would otherwise produce $\infty \times 0 = \text{NaN}$ are handled via selective replacement (\texttt{torch.where}) prior to the softmax, and any layer producing NaN outputs is skipped from the sparsity loss computation.
40	
41	\item \textbf{Random.} KV positions (excluding BOS) are evicted uniformly at random, providing a strategy-agnostic baseline. Head pruning under the random condition selects heads via \texttt{torch.randperm} rather than by importance.
42	\end{itemize}
43	
44	\paragraph{Head pruning.} Under importance-based eviction, heads are ranked by their Frobenius norm across the full attention matrix $\mathbf{A}_\ell \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times T \times T}$ per layer $\ell$, and the bottom-$s$ fraction is masked. Under random eviction, heads are selected uniformly at random.
45	
46	
47	\subsection{Phase Segmentation}
48	\label{sec:phase-seg}
49	
50	We segment each generated sequence into three \emph{reasoning phases} based on the local attention sparsity of each token position. For each query position $i$, we compute per-head sparsity as the fraction of attention weights falling below $0.01 \times \max_j a_{i,h,j}$, then average across heads to obtain a scalar sparsity value per position. The resulting sparsity trajectory is partitioned into terciles via quantile boundaries: \emph{low-sparsity} (bottom third, corresponding to focused attention during structured computation), \emph{mid-sparsity}, and \emph{high-sparsity} (top third, corresponding to diffuse attention during exploratory reasoning). Contiguous segments shorter than $\texttt{min\_phase\_length}=10$ tokens are merged into adjacent phases to suppress noise.
51	
52	
53	\subsection{Metrics}
54	\label{sec:metrics}
55	
56	\paragraph{Perplexity.} For each sparsity condition $c \in \{d, a, k, b\}$ and each phase, we compute segment-level perplexity as
57	$\text{PPL}_c = \exp\!\bigl(\tfrac{1}{|I|}\sum_{i \in I} \mathcal{L}_c(x_i)\bigr)$,
58	where $I$ is the set of token indices belonging to the phase and $\mathcal{L}_c(x_i)$ is the per-token cross-entropy loss under condition $c$.
59	
60	\paragraph{Interaction Index.} The interaction index quantifies the synergistic (super-additive) effect of compound sparsity beyond the sum of individual interventions:
61	\begin{equation}
62	\label{eq:ii}
63	    \mathrm{II} = \frac{\text{PPL}_b}{\text{PPL}_d} - \frac{\text{PPL}_a}{\text{PPL}_d} - \frac{\text{PPL}_k}{\text{PPL}_d} + 1.
64	\end{equation}
65	When $\mathrm{II} > 0$, the two sparsity mechanisms amplify each other; $\mathrm{II} = 0$ indicates additive (independent) degradation.
66	
67	\paragraph{Severity Gradient.} To measure how the interaction varies across reasoning phases, we define the severity gradient:
68	\begin{equation}
69	\label{eq:gradient}
70	    G = \frac{\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\,\textit{low}}}{\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\,\textit{high}}},
71	\end{equation}
72	where $\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\,\textit{low}}$ and $\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\,\textit{high}}$ are the median interaction indices over the low-sparsity and high-sparsity phases, respectively. We report medians rather than means because the II distribution is heavily right-skewed (mean/median ratios up to 43:1 at $s{=}0.30$), making the median a more robust central tendency estimator.
73	
74	
75	\subsection{Statistical Analysis}
76	\label{sec:stats}
77	
78	All confidence intervals and significance tests are computed via the nonparametric bootstrap with $B = 1{,}000$ resamples \cite{efron1993bootstrap}.
79	
80	\paragraph{Per-problem bootstrap.} For each sparsity level and strategy, we resample the 50 per-problem II values with replacement and compute the mean of each resample, yielding a 95\% percentile confidence interval for the population mean II.
81	
82	\paragraph{Paired bootstrap.} To test whether the severity gradient differs between importance-based and random eviction, we pair observations by problem (same problem, same sparsity level) and bootstrap the difference in gradients. This controls for problem-level variance in difficulty and sequence length.
83	
84	\paragraph{Unpaired bootstrap.} We additionally compute per-strategy gradient confidence intervals without pairing, to verify that the importance-based gradient is significantly greater than 1 (i.e., phase modulation exists) independently of the random baseline.
85	
86	All tests yield $p < 0.0001$ at every sparsity level, confirming that the observed phase--strategy interactions are not artifacts of sampling variability.\footnote{Experiments were conducted on a server with 4$\times$ NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada 96\,GB GPUs, with one model--sparsity configuration per GPU.}
87

Compound sparsity（attention head pruning + KV cache eviction）的 severity 不是固定常数——它是 eviction strategy 和 reasoning phase 交互的涌现属性。Importance-based eviction 在 low-sparsity reasoning phase 产生 11-42× severity amplification（problem-level bootstrap），而 random eviction 保持 ~1× 平坦。这一发现挑战了 compound degradation 均匀分布的隐含假设。

**⚠️ 数字基准**：本文件中的具体数字（gradient magnitude, crossover values）基于 fp16 problem-level bootstrap 结果。bf16 重跑完成后必须统一更新。segment-level 估计（12-75×）已弃用，仅在被明确标注时作为参考。

## Narrative Arc

Compound sparsity 是高效 LLM 推理的实用部署需求，但 prior work（SparK, Ada-KV, SLiM）将 compound interaction 视为均匀超可加。我们发现 severity 是 strategy × phase 交互的涌现属性：importance eviction 在 distributed-attention phase 剧烈放大 compound degradation（problem-level gradient 11-42×），而 random eviction 在所有 phase 保持平坦（~1×）。我们通过 entropy-discrimination collapse 机制解释这一现象：head pruning → attention 重分布 → importance score 的判别力崩塌 → importance eviction 退化为有偏伪随机。这一发现为 phase-aware sparsity allocation 提供了动机。

**Framing 硬约束（D015）**：
- MUST: "emergent phase-strategy interaction"
- MUST NOT: "importance metric limitation / importance is broken"

## Core Claims

| ID | Claim | Status | Key Evidence |
|----|-------|--------|-------------|
| C1 | Compound sparsity severity is strategy-dependent | confirmed | importance gradient 11-42× (problem-level) vs random ~1×. 待 bf16 数据更新 |
| C2 | Severity is phase-modulated (amplified in low-sparsity phase) | confirmed | low phase >> high phase at all 4 sparsity levels. Problem-level: 11.53→11.05→35.72→41.92（s015→s020 非严格单调，bf16 数据可能改变趋势。论文措辞用 "increases with sparsity" 而非 "monotonically increases"） |
| C3 | Phase-strategy crossover exists | confirmed | s=0.25: importance high_phase=0.584 < random=3.002, importance low_phase=30.903 > random=2.915 |
| C4 | Entropy-discrimination collapse explains the mechanism | partially_confirmed | Conceptual argument solid; empirical attention entropy data not yet collected |
| C5 | Finding generalizes across models (same arch, different training) | pending | Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct experiments in progress. Note: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B 和 Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct 共享 Qwen2ForCausalLM 架构，区别在训练方式（distillation vs instruction tuning）。是 cross-model 而非 cross-architecture replication。 |
| C6 | Severity gradient is sub-exponential | confirmed | Growth rate decreasing: 2.24×→1.84×→1.42× |

## Anticipated Reviewer Concerns

### RC1: Generalizability — 7B models only, single benchmark
- **预期质疑**: "Results on two 7B models and MATH-500 only. How do we know this generalizes to larger models or other reasoning tasks?"
- **应对**: Cross-model replication (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B + Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) 控制架构变量、隔离训练方式影响（distillation vs instruction tuning）。注意：两模型共享 Qwen2ForCausalLM 架构，不能 claim 跨架构泛化。MATH-500 是 standard benchmark。Limitations 必须诚实声明：(1) 同架构不同训练，不是跨架构；(2) 7B scale only；(3) 单 benchmark。机制解释 (entropy-discrimination collapse) 原则上 architecture-agnostic，但未实证验证。
- **实验支撑**: C5 (Qwen cross-model). 若需加强可扩展到不同架构（如 LLaMA/Mistral），但 11 天 deadline 内不现实

### RC2: Mechanism — entropy-discrimination collapse 缺乏直接测量
- **预期质疑**: "The mechanism is conceptual. Where is the empirical evidence for entropy increase and discrimination collapse?"
- **应对**: 如果有 GPU 预算，可以直接测量 pruned vs unpruned 的 attention entropy 和 importance score 分布。目前 C4 status = partially_confirmed，需要决定是否投入 GPU 时间做 direct measurement。
- **实验支撑**: 可选 ablation：测量 attention entropy pre/post pruning × phase

### RC3: Practical impact — 没有 throughput 数据
- **预期质疑**: "No wall-clock or throughput measurements. Is the severity amplification reflected in actual inference speed?"
- **应对**: 本文定位是 empirical finding paper（发现 + 机制解释），不是 method paper。Throughput 不是 claim 的一部分。Discussion 中明确 phase-gated controller 作为 future direction。
- **实验支撑**: 不需要额外实验

### RC4: Statistical rigor — bootstrap 是否足够
- **预期质疑**: "Per-problem bootstrap with 50 problems — sufficient sample size?"
- **应对**: B=10000 iterations, all p=0.0000, CI 不跨零。fp16 下实际配对数为 16-22/50（NaN 过滤后），bf16 预期恢复到 ~45-50 配对。bf16 数据到手后需重新验证统计效力。可在 appendix 补充 per-problem 分布图。
- **实验支撑**: fp16 bootstrap 已完成；bf16 bootstrap 待重做（plan_008）

### RC5: Novelty — prior work 是否已覆盖 phase-dependent sparsity
- **预期质疑**: "ThinKV and phase-aware methods already consider phase. What's new?"
- **应对**: Prior work 在单轴上分析 phase（ThinKV: phase-aware eviction）或 compound（SparK: joint compression）。没有工作同时分析 compound × phase × strategy 的三维交互。Crossover 现象（同一 strategy 在不同 phase 方向反转）是全新发现。
- **实验支撑**: C3 (crossover), Related Work §2 的 gap 分析

## Paper Positioning

**类型**: Empirical finding paper（非 method paper）
**核心贡献**:
1. 发现 compound sparsity severity 的 strategy × phase 交互
2. 量化 severity gradient（problem-level 11-42×, 待 bf16 更新）和 crossover 现象
3. 提出 entropy-discrimination collapse 机制解释
4. Cross-model replication 验证泛化性

# LaTeX 论文写作全流程

ML/AI 顶会论文从草稿到投稿的完整指南。整合 Orchestra Research、VibeSkills、claim2evidence 三方最佳实践。

---

## 1. 工作模式

开始前选择模式：

| 模式 | 说明 | 适用 |
|------|------|------|
| **Build** | 从实验笔记/结果/代码生成论文 | 新稿 |
| **Improve** | 改写已有章节，强化论证 | 修改稿 |
| **Audit** | 输出风险列表 + 缺失证据 + 修复建议 | 投前检查 |

---

## 2. Claim-Evidence 方法论

**核心原则：论文是一个有中心贡献的故事，不是实验的堆砌。**

### 2.1 一句话贡献

在写任何内容之前，必须能用一句话说清贡献。如果不能，说明还没准备好写论文。

### 2.2 Claim-Evidence Map

为每个 contribution 建立 claim→evidence 映射表：

| Contribution | Claim | Evidence | Table/Figure |
|-------------|-------|----------|-------------|
| C1: 方法 X 在 Y 上 SOTA | 比所有 baseline 高 ≥2% | 5-seed 平均，p<0.05 | Table 1 |
| C2: 消融证明 Z 是关键 | 去掉 Z 后掉 >5% | 消融实验 | Table 2 |
| C3: 计算效率 | 比 baseline 快 3× | FLOPs + wall-clock | Figure 3 |

**没有直接证据支撑的 claim 必须删除或降级为 discussion。**

### 2.3 章节起草顺序

```
1. Introduction + Experiments（先确定 claim 和 evidence）
2. Method（评估问题稳定后再写细节）
3. Related Work

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

% TODO: §7 full draft pending Phase 4. Currently contains only the

\paragraph{On the predictability of phase-modulated severity.}
One might argue that the qualitative direction of our findings is intuitive: in low-sparsity phases, attention distributes broadly across many tokens, so importance scores carry less discriminative signal, and importance-based eviction should degrade.
We do not dispute this intuition.
The surprise lies in the quantitative structure of the interaction, which is not predictable from first principles alone.

First, the \emph{magnitude} of the severity gradient---$11$--$42\times$ amplification % PENDING-BF16
across sparsity levels (Table~\ref{tab:bootstrap})---far exceeds what a naive ``less discriminative $\Rightarrow$ somewhat worse'' argument would predict.
A reviewer expecting a $2$--$3\times$ effect would find an order-of-magnitude amplification difficult to anticipate without measurement.
Second, the gradient is \emph{phase-specific}: compound interaction concentrates in low-sparsity phases while high-sparsity phases exhibit near-additive behavior ($\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\text{high}} < 1$ at all sparsity levels). % PENDING-BF16
This asymmetry means that importance-based eviction is not uniformly fragile---it is selectively fragile in a phase-dependent manner.
Third, and most strikingly, a \emph{crossover} emerges: at $s \geq 0.25$, importance-based eviction \emph{outperforms} random eviction in high-sparsity phases ($\widetilde{\mathrm{II}} = 0.58$ vs.\ $3.00$) % PENDING-BF16
yet \emph{underperforms} dramatically in low-sparsity phases ($\widetilde{\mathrm{II}} = 30.9$ vs.\ $2.9$). % PENDING-BF16
The same strategy reverses direction across phases---a phenomenon that cannot be derived from the observation that ``importance scores are noisier when attention is diffuse.''

1	% Section 5.1: Phase-Modulated Severity Gradient
2	% Data source: v6_importance_s015/s020/s025/s030, mvp_v5_random_s015/s020/s025/s030
3	% All numeric values are from fp16 runs; bf16 replication pending.
4	
5	\subsection{Phase-Modulated Severity Gradient}
6	\label{sec:severity-gradient}
7	
8	Under importance-based eviction, compound interaction severity varies by an order of magnitude across reasoning phases:
9	the severity gradient $G$ (Eq.~\eqref{eq:gradient}) ranges from $11.5\times$ at $s{=}0.15$ to% PENDING-BF16
10	$41.9\times$ at $s{=}0.30$% PENDING-BF16
11	(paired bootstrap, $B{=}10{,}000$; Table~\ref{tab:bootstrap}).
12	Random eviction yields a flat gradient of $G \approx 0.7$--$1.8\times$% PENDING-BF16
13	across all sparsity levels (Table~\ref{tab:main-results}), confirming that phase modulation is specific to importance-based strategies rather than an inherent property of compound sparsity.
14	Figure~\ref{fig:hero} visualizes the divergent severity profiles of the two strategies.
15	
16	%%% Table 1: Main results %%%
17	\begin{table}[t]
18	\centering
19	\small
20	\caption{Median Interaction Index ($\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}$) by reasoning phase and severity gradient $G$ for importance-based and random eviction on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (50 MATH-500 problems).
21	$G$ for importance-based eviction is estimated via paired problem-level bootstrap ($B{=}10{,}000$);
22	$G$ for random eviction is the simple median ratio $\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\textit{low}} / \widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\textit{high}}$.
23	Higher $G$ indicates stronger phase modulation.
24	All values from \texttt{float16} runs; \texttt{bfloat16} replication pending.}
25	\label{tab:main-results}
26	\begin{tabular}{@{}llrrrr@{}}
27	\toprule
28	Strategy & $s$ & $\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\textit{high}}$ & $\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\textit{mid}}$ & $\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\textit{low}}$ & $G$ \\
29	\midrule
30	Importance & 0.15 & 0.23 & 0.74 & 2.88 & \textbf{11.53} \\ % PENDING-BF16
31	Random     & 0.15 & 0.16 & 0.25 & 0.18 & 1.14 \\ % PENDING-BF16
32	\addlinespace
33	Importance & 0.20 & 0.34 & 1.67 & 9.25 & \textbf{11.05} \\ % PENDING-BF16
34	Random     & 0.20 & 0.32 & 0.46 & 0.59 & 1.84 \\ % PENDING-BF16
35	\addlinespace
36	Importance & 0.25 & 0.66 & 5.31 & 24.16 & \textbf{35.72} \\ % PENDING-BF16
37	Random     & 0.25 & 3.00 & 2.98 & 2.91 & 0.97 \\ % PENDING-BF16
38	\addlinespace
39	Importance & 0.30 & 0.88 & 7.27 & 34.69 & \textbf{41.92} \\ % PENDING-BF16
40	Random     & 0.30 & 5.38 & 5.89 & 3.78 & 0.70 \\ % PENDING-BF16
41	\bottomrule
42	\end{tabular}
43	\end{table}
44	
45	%%% Walking through Table 1 %%%
46	
47	\paragraph{Importance-based eviction.}
48	The low-sparsity phase---where attention distributes broadly across the context---bears the brunt of compound interaction.
49	Its median II rises from $2.88$ at $s{=}0.15$ to $34.69$ at $s{=}0.30$, a $12\times$ increase,% PENDING-BF16
50	while the high-sparsity phase median grows only from $0.23$ to $0.88$ ($3.8\times$).% PENDING-BF16
51	This asymmetric scaling drives $G$ upward from ${\sim}12\times$ to ${\sim}42\times$ as sparsity increases.% PENDING-BF16
52	The mid-sparsity phase tracks intermediate values, rising from $0.74$ to $7.27$,% PENDING-BF16
53	consistent with a smooth severity gradient across phases rather than a binary high/low dichotomy.
54	
55	\paragraph{Random eviction.}
56	Under random eviction, the median II shows no systematic ordering across phases.
57	At $s{=}0.30$, for instance, $\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\textit{high}} = 5.38$ exceeds% PENDING-BF16
58	$\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\textit{low}} = 3.78$,% PENDING-BF16
59	yielding $G = 0.70$---the opposite direction of the importance-based pattern.% PENDING-BF16
60	Across all four sparsity levels, the random gradient remains within $0.70$--$1.84\times$,% PENDING-BF16
61	confirming the absence of phase modulation.
62	
63	%%% Table 2: Bootstrap CIs %%%
64	\begin{table}[t]
65	\centering
66	\small
67	\caption{Bootstrap severity gradient estimates ($B{=}10{,}000$) for importance-based eviction.
68	Paired estimates control for problem-level variance by computing $G$ from matched high- and low-phase observations within each problem ($n_{\text{paired}} \in [16, 22]$);
69	unpaired estimates use all available observations per phase ($n_{\textit{high}} \in [40, 43]$, $n_{\textit{low}} \in [20, 24]$).
70	All $p$-values test $H_0\!: G \leq 1$.
71	All values from \texttt{float16} runs; \texttt{bfloat16} replication pending.}
72	\label{tab:bootstrap}
73	\begin{tabular}{@{}rrlrl@{}}
74	\toprule
75	$s$ & $G_{\text{paired}}$ & 95\% CI & $G_{\text{unpaired}}$ & 95\% CI \\
76	\midrule
77	0.15 & 11.53 & $[3.49,\; 23.78]$ & 12.69 & $[4.96,\; 28.45]$ \\ % PENDING-BF16
78	0.20 & 11.05 & $[5.42,\; 69.27]$ & 27.60 & $[6.55,\; 75.16]$ \\ % PENDING-BF16
79	0.25 & 35.72 & $[9.52,\; 101.54]$ & 36.38 & $[13.19,\; 97.61]$ \\ % PENDING-BF16
80	0.30 & 41.92 & $[19.14,\; 299.76]$ & 39.28 & $[21.87,\; 129.59]$ \\ % PENDING-BF16
81	\bottomrule
82	\multicolumn{5}{@{}l}{\footnotesize All $p(G \leq 1) < 10^{-4}$ for both paired and unpaired tests.}
83	\end{tabular}
84	\end{table}
85	
86	%%% Statistical significance %%%
87	
88	At every sparsity level, the 95\% bootstrap confidence interval for $G$ lies entirely above 1,
89	with lower bounds ranging from $3.49$ (paired, $s{=}0.15$)% PENDING-BF16
90	to $21.87$ (unpaired, $s{=}0.30$),% PENDING-BF16
91	and all $p < 10^{-4}$ (Table~\ref{tab:bootstrap}).
92	The paired and unpaired estimates agree in direction and magnitude, indicating that the gradient is robust to whether the comparison is within-problem or across the full sample.
93	
94	%%% Sub-exponential growth %%%
95	
96	The gradient increases with sparsity but exhibits diminishing returns:
97	$G$ dips slightly from $11.53\times$ at $s{=}0.15$ to $11.05\times$ at $s{=}0.20$% PENDING-BF16
98	before rising sharply to $35.72\times$ at $s{=}0.25$,% PENDING-BF16
99	then leveling off at $41.92\times$ at $s{=}0.30$% PENDING-BF16
100	(a $1.2\times$ marginal increase over the preceding $3.2\times$ jump).% PENDING-BF16
101	This sub-linear scaling at higher sparsity suggests a natural ceiling on severity amplification, possibly reflecting a floor effect in the high-sparsity phase where concentrated attention already protects the most critical tokens.
102	
103	%%% Random baseline interpretation %%%
104	
105	The flat gradient under random eviction serves as a critical control.

% Data source: v6_importance_s015/s020/s025/s030, mvp_v5_random_s015/s020/s025/s030
% All numeric values are from fp16 runs; bf16 replication pending.

\subsection{Phase-Modulated Severity Gradient}
\label{sec:severity-gradient}

Under importance-based eviction, compound interaction severity varies by an order of magnitude across reasoning phases:
the severity gradient $G$ (Eq.~\eqref{eq:gradient}) ranges from $11.5\times$ at $s{=}0.15$ to% PENDING-BF16
$41.9\times$ at $s{=}0.30$% PENDING-BF16
(paired bootstrap, $B{=}10{,}000$; Table~\ref{tab:bootstrap}).
Random eviction yields a flat gradient of $G \approx 0.7$--$1.8\times$% PENDING-BF16
across all sparsity levels (Table~\ref{tab:main-results}), confirming that phase modulation is specific to importance-based strategies rather than an inherent property of compound sparsity.
Figure~\ref{fig:hero} visualizes the divergent severity profiles of the two strategies.

%%% Table 1: Main results %%%
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Median Interaction Index ($\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}$) by reasoning phase and severity gradient $G$ for importance-based and random eviction on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (50 MATH-500 problems).
$G$ for importance-based eviction is estimated via paired problem-level bootstrap ($B{=}10{,}000$);
$G$ for random eviction is the simple median ratio $\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\textit{low}} / \widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\textit{high}}$.
Higher $G$ indicates stronger phase modulation.
All values from \texttt{float16} runs; \texttt{bfloat16} replication pending.}
\label{tab:main-results}
\begin{tabular}{@{}llrrrr@{}}
\toprule
Strategy & $s$ & $\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\textit{high}}$ & $\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\textit{mid}}$ & $\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\textit{low}}$ & $G$ \\
\midrule
Importance & 0.15 & 0.23 & 0.74 & 2.88 & \textbf{11.53} \\ % PENDING-BF16
Random     & 0.15 & 0.16 & 0.25 & 0.18 & 1.14 \\ % PENDING-BF16
\addlinespace
Importance & 0.20 & 0.34 & 1.67 & 9.25 & \textbf{11.05} \\ % PENDING-BF16
Random     & 0.20 & 0.32 & 0.46 & 0.59 & 1.84 \\ % PENDING-BF16
\addlinespace
Importance & 0.25 & 0.66 & 5.31 & 24.16 & \textbf{35.72} \\ % PENDING-BF16
Random     & 0.25 & 3.00 & 2.98 & 2.91 & 0.97 \\ % PENDING-BF16
\addlinespace
Importance & 0.30 & 0.88 & 7.27 & 34.69 & \textbf{41.92} \\ % PENDING-BF16
Random     & 0.30 & 5.38 & 5.89 & 3.78 & 0.70 \\ % PENDING-BF16
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

%%% Walking through Table 1 %%%

\paragraph{Importance-based eviction.}
The low-sparsity phase---where attention distributes broadly across the context---bears the brunt of compound interaction.
Its median II rises from $2.88$ at $s{=}0.15$ to $34.69$ at $s{=}0.30$, a $12\times$ increase,% PENDING-BF16
while the high-sparsity phase median grows only from $0.23$ to $0.88$ ($3.8\times$).% PENDING-BF16
This asymmetric scaling drives $G$ upward from ${\sim}12\times$ to ${\sim}42\times$ as sparsity increases.% PENDING-BF16
The mid-sparsity phase tracks intermediate values, rising from $0.74$ to $7.27$,% PENDING-BF16
consistent with a smooth severity gradient across phases rather than a binary high/low dichotomy.

\paragraph{Random eviction.}
Under random eviction, the median II shows no systematic ordering across phases.
At $s{=}0.30$, for instance, $\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\textit{high}} = 5.38$ exceeds% PENDING-BF16
$\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\textit{low}} = 3.78$,% PENDING-BF16
yielding $G = 0.70$---the opposite direction of the importance-based pattern.% PENDING-BF16
Across all four sparsity levels, the random gradient remains within $0.70$--$1.84\times$,% PENDING-BF16
confirming the absence of phase modulation.

%%% Table 2: Bootstrap CIs %%%
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Bootstrap severity gradient estimates ($B{=}10{,}000$) for importance-based eviction.
Paired estimates control for problem-level variance by computing $G$ from matched high- and low-phase observations within each problem ($n_{\text{paired}} \in [16, 22]$);
unpaired estimates use all available observations per phase ($n_{\textit{high}} \in [40, 43]$, $n_{\textit{low}} \in [20, 24]$).
All $p$-values test $H_0\!: G \leq 1$.
All values from \texttt{float16} runs; \texttt{bfloat16} replication pending.}
\label{tab:bootstrap}
\begin{tabular}{@{}rrlrl@{}}
\toprule
$s$ & $G_{\text{paired}}$ & 95\% CI & $G_{\text{unpaired}}$ & 95\% CI \\
\midrule
0.15 & 11.53 & $[3.49,\; 23.78]$ & 12.69 & $[4.96,\; 28.45]$ \\ % PENDING-BF16
0.20 & 11.05 & $[5.42,\; 69.27]$ & 27.60 & $[6.55,\; 75.16]$ \\ % PENDING-BF16
0.25 & 35.72 & $[9.52,\; 101.54]$ & 36.38 & $[13.19,\; 97.61]$ \\ % PENDING-BF16
0.30 & 41.92 & $[19.14,\; 299.76]$ & 39.28 & $[21.87,\; 129.59]$ \\ % PENDING-BF16
\bottomrule
\multicolumn{5}{@{}l}{\footnotesize All $p(G \leq 1) < 10^{-4}$ for both paired and unpaired tests.}
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

%%% Statistical significance %%%

At every sparsity level, the 95\% bootstrap confidence interval for $G$ lies entirely above 1,
with lower bounds ranging from $3.49$ (paired, $s{=}0.15$)% PENDING-BF16
to $21.87$ (unpaired, $s{=}0.30$),% PENDING-BF16
and all $p < 10^{-4}$ (Table~\ref{tab:bootstrap}).
The paired and unpaired estimates agree in direction and magnitude, indicating that the gradient is robust to whether the comparison is within-problem or across the full sample.

%%% Sub-exponential growth %%%

The gradient increases with sparsity but exhibits diminishing returns:
$G$ dips slightly from $11.53\times$ at $s{=}0.15$ to $11.05\times$ at $s{=}0.20$% PENDING-BF16
before rising sharply to $35.72\times$ at $s{=}0.25$,% PENDING-BF16
then leveling off at $41.92\times$ at $s{=}0.30$% PENDING-BF16
(a $1.2\times$ marginal increase over the preceding $3.2\times$ jump).% PENDING-BF16
This sub-linear scaling at higher sparsity suggests a natural ceiling on severity amplification, possibly reflecting a floor effect in the high-sparsity phase where concentrated attention already protects the most critical tokens.

%%% Random baseline interpretation %%%

demonstrates that the observed gradient is an emergent property of the interaction between importance-based eviction and reasoning phase structure, not a generic feature of compound sparsity.

%%% Figures %%%
\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig1_hero.pdf}
\caption{Severity gradient ($G$) as a function of sparsity level $s$.
Importance-based eviction (solid) exhibits a gradient that increases with sparsity from% PENDING-BF16
$11.5\times$ to $41.9\times$, while random eviction (dashed) remains flat near $1\times$.% PENDING-BF16
Shaded regions denote 95\% bootstrap confidence intervals ($B{=}10{,}000$).}
\label{fig:hero}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig4_bootstrap.pdf}

All CIs lie entirely above $G{=}1$ (vertical dashed line), confirming significant phase modulation at every sparsity level ($p < 10^{-4}$).}
\label{fig:bootstrap}
\end{figure}

% All numeric values are from fp16 runs; bf16 replication pending.

\subsection{Phase-Modulated Severity Gradient}
\label{sec:severity-gradient}

Under importance-based eviction, compound interaction severity varies by an order of magnitude across reasoning phases:
the severity gradient $G$ (Eq.~\eqref{eq:gradient}) ranges from $11.5\times$ at $s{=}0.15$ to% PENDING-BF16
$41.9\times$ at $s{=}0.30$% PENDING-BF16
(paired bootstrap, $B{=}10{,}000$; Table~\ref{tab:bootstrap}).
Random eviction yields a flat gradient of $G \approx 0.7$--$1.8\times$% PENDING-BF16
across all sparsity levels (Table~\ref{tab:main-results}), confirming that phase modulation is specific to importance-based strategies rather than an inherent property of compound sparsity.
Figure~\ref{fig:hero} visualizes the divergent severity profiles of the two strategies.

%%% Table 1: Main results %%%
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Median Interaction Index ($\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}$) by reasoning phase and severity gradient $G$ for importance-based and random eviction on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (50 MATH-500 problems).
$G$ for importance-based eviction is estimated via paired problem-level bootstrap ($B{=}10{,}000$);
$G$ for random eviction is the simple median ratio $\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\textit{low}} / \widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\textit{high}}$.
Higher $G$ indicates stronger phase modulation.
All values from \texttt{float16} runs; \texttt{bfloat16} replication pending.}
\label{tab:main-results}
\begin{tabular}{@{}llrrrr@{}}
\toprule
Strategy & $s$ & $\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\textit{high}}$ & $\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\textit{mid}}$ & $\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\textit{low}}$ & $G$ \\
\midrule
Importance & 0.15 & 0.23 & 0.74 & 2.88 & \textbf{11.53} \\ % PENDING-BF16
Random     & 0.15 & 0.16 & 0.25 & 0.18 & 1.14 \\ % PENDING-BF16
\addlinespace
Importance & 0.20 & 0.34 & 1.67 & 9.25 & \textbf{11.05} \\ % PENDING-BF16
Random     & 0.20 & 0.32 & 0.46 & 0.59 & 1.84 \\ % PENDING-BF16
\addlinespace
Importance & 0.25 & 0.66 & 5.31 & 24.16 & \textbf{35.72} \\ % PENDING-BF16
Random     & 0.25 & 3.00 & 2.98 & 2.91 & 0.97 \\ % PENDING-BF16
\addlinespace
Importance & 0.30 & 0.88 & 7.27 & 34.69 & \textbf{41.92} \\ % PENDING-BF16
Random     & 0.30 & 5.38 & 5.89 & 3.78 & 0.70 \\ % PENDING-BF16
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

%%% Walking through Table 1 %%%

\paragraph{Importance-based eviction.}
The low-sparsity phase---where attention distributes broadly across the context---bears the brunt of compound interaction.
Its median II rises from $2.88$ at $s{=}0.15$ to $34.69$ at $s{=}0.30$, a $12\times$ increase,% PENDING-BF16
while the high-sparsity phase median grows only from $0.23$ to $0.88$ ($3.8\times$).% PENDING-BF16
This asymmetric scaling drives $G$ upward from ${\sim}12\times$ to ${\sim}42\times$ as sparsity increases.% PENDING-BF16
The mid-sparsity phase tracks intermediate values, rising from $0.74$ to $7.27$,% PENDING-BF16
consistent with a smooth severity gradient across phases rather than a binary high/low dichotomy.

\paragraph{Random eviction.}
Under random eviction, the median II shows no systematic ordering across phases.
At $s{=}0.30$, for instance, $\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\textit{high}} = 5.38$ exceeds% PENDING-BF16
$\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\textit{low}} = 3.78$,% PENDING-BF16
yielding $G = 0.70$---the opposite direction of the importance-based pattern.% PENDING-BF16
Across all four sparsity levels, the random gradient remains within $0.70$--$1.84\times$,% PENDING-BF16
confirming the absence of phase modulation.

%%% Table 2: Bootstrap CIs %%%
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Bootstrap severity gradient estimates ($B{=}10{,}000$) for importance-based eviction.
Paired estimates control for problem-level variance by computing $G$ from matched high- and low-phase observations within each problem ($n_{\text{paired}} \in [16, 22]$);
unpaired estimates use all available observations per phase ($n_{\textit{high}} \in [40, 43]$, $n_{\textit{low}} \in [20, 24]$).
All $p$-values test $H_0\!: G \leq 1$.
All values from \texttt{float16} runs; \texttt{bfloat16} replication pending.}
\label{tab:bootstrap}
\begin{tabular}{@{}rrlrl@{}}
\toprule
$s$ & $G_{\text{paired}}$ & 95\% CI & $G_{\text{unpaired}}$ & 95\% CI \\
\midrule
0.15 & 11.53 & $[3.49,\; 23.78]$ & 12.69 & $[4.96,\; 28.45]$ \\ % PENDING-BF16
0.20 & 11.05 & $[5.42,\; 69.27]$ & 27.60 & $[6.55,\; 75.16]$ \\ % PENDING-BF16
0.25 & 35.72 & $[9.52,\; 101.54]$ & 36.38 & $[13.19,\; 97.61]$ \\ % PENDING-BF16
0.30 & 41.92 & $[19.14,\; 299.76]$ & 39.28 & $[21.87,\; 129.59]$ \\ % PENDING-BF16
\bottomrule
\multicolumn{5}{@{}l}{\footnotesize All $p(G \leq 1) < 10^{-4}$ for both paired and unpaired tests.}
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

%%% Statistical significance %%%

At every sparsity level, the 95\% bootstrap confidence interval for $G$ lies entirely above 1,
with lower bounds ranging from $3.49$ (paired, $s{=}0.15$)% PENDING-BF16
to $21.87$ (unpaired, $s{=}0.30$),% PENDING-BF16
and all $p < 10^{-4}$ (Table~\ref{tab:bootstrap}).
The paired and unpaired estimates agree in direction and magnitude, indicating that the gradient is robust to whether the comparison is within-problem or across the full sample.

%%% Sub-exponential growth %%%

The gradient increases with sparsity but exhibits diminishing returns:
$G$ dips slightly from $11.53\times$ at $s{=}0.15$ to $11.05\times$ at $s{=}0.20$% PENDING-BF16
before rising sharply to $35.72\times$ at $s{=}0.25$,% PENDING-BF16
then leveling off at $41.92\times$ at $s{=}0.30$% PENDING-BF16
(a $1.2\times$ marginal increase over the preceding $3.2\times$ jump).% PENDING-BF16
This sub-linear scaling at higher sparsity suggests a natural ceiling on severity amplification, possibly reflecting a floor effect in the high-sparsity phase where concentrated attention already protects the most critical tokens.

%%% Random baseline interpretation %%%

The flat gradient under random eviction serves as a critical control.
If the severity gradient were a trivial consequence of compound sparsity---for instance, because low-sparsity phases have broadly distributed attention that makes any eviction criterion less discriminative---then random eviction should also exhibit phase modulation.
The absence of such modulation ($G \in [0.70, 1.84]$ across all sparsity levels; Table~\ref{tab:main-results})% PENDING-BF16
demonstrates that the observed gradient is an emergent property of the interaction between importance-based eviction and reasoning phase structure, not a generic feature of compound sparsity.

%%% Figures %%%
\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig1_hero.pdf}
\caption{Severity gradient ($G$) as a function of sparsity level $s$.
Importance-based eviction (solid) exhibits a gradient that increases with sparsity from% PENDING-BF16
$11.5\times$ to $41.9\times$, while random eviction (dashed) remains flat near $1\times$.% PENDING-BF16
Shaded regions denote 95\% bootstrap confidence intervals ($B{=}10{,}000$).}
\label{fig:hero}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig4_bootstrap.pdf}
\caption{Forest plot of bootstrap severity gradient estimates for importance-based eviction.
Horizontal bars show 95\% percentile CIs; diamonds mark point estimates.
All CIs lie entirely above $G{=}1$ (vertical dashed line), confirming significant phase modulation at every sparsity level ($p < 10^{-4}$).}
\label{fig:bootstrap}
\end{figure}

Results\\\"\\n      summary: >\\n        Main finding: importance gradient 12.8-74.9× (median) monotonically increasing with sparsity,\\n        random gradient ~1×.     - id: abstract
      title: Abstract
      summary: >
        Compound sparsity (head pruning + KV cache eviction) is assumed to degrade uniformly.
        We show the interaction is strategy-dependent and phase-modulated: importance-based eviction
        exhibits 12-75× severity amplification in low-sparsity reasoning phases, while random eviction

      title: "1. Introduction"

        emergent property of the interaction between eviction strategy and reasoning phase.
        Preview crossover phenomenon and mechanism. State contributions.
      length: 1 page
      key_claims:

        — none analyzes phase × strategy interaction. (2) KV cache eviction (Ada-KV, DefensiveKV,
        SnapKV, NACL) — importance fragility noted but not phase-conditioned. (3) Phase-aware
        inference (ThinKV, PagedEviction, reasoning dynamics) — single-axis, no compound interaction.
      length: 0.75 page
      key_refs:

        Define compound sparsity (attention head pruning ⊗ KV cache eviction). Define Interaction
        Index (II) measuring super/sub-additivity. Define phase segmentation via ThinKV-style
        token-ratio method. Formalize the research question: is II constant across phases and strategies?
      length: 1 page
      subsections:
        - "3.1 Compound Sparsity Formulation"
        - "3.2 Interaction Index"
        - "3.3 Phase Segmentation"

    - id: methodology

        Models (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), dataset (MATH-500 subset, 50 problems),
        sparsity levels (s=0.15/0.20/0.25/0.30), eviction strategies (importance-based cumulative
        attention with position normalization, random), metrics (PPL, II, gradient), hardware.
        Statistical method: per-problem bootstrap CI (B=10000), paired and unpaired.
      length: 1 page

    - id: results
      title: "5. Results"
      summary: >
        Main finding: importance gradient 12.8-74.9× (median) monotonically increasing with sparsity,
        random gradient ~1×. Bootstrap CI all significant (p=0.0000). Crossover: importance safer
        than random in high-sparsity phase but dramatically worse in low-sparsity phase.

        - "5.2 Strategy-Dependent Crossover"
        - "5.3 Cross-Model Replication"

      title: "6. Analysis: Entropy-Discrimination Collapse"
      summary: >
        Mechanistic explanation: head pruning → surviving heads attend more uniformly → importance
        score entropy increases → discrimination between important/unimportant KV entries collapses →
        importance-based eviction degrades to biased pseudo-random in distributed-attention phases.
        This is phase-dependent because reasoning phases have more distributed attention.
      length: 1 page

      length: 0.5 page

      summary: >
        Compound sparsity severity is an emergent property of strategy × phase interaction.

## Writing Plan — Phase-Gated Compound Sparsity
## 最后更新: 2026-05-14

# ============================================================
# 投稿目标
# ============================================================
target:
  venue: EMNLP 2026 ARR
  deadline: 2026-05-25
  days_remaining: 11
  format: long paper (8 pages + references + appendix)
  anonymization: ARR double-blind

# ============================================================
# Paper Outline
# ============================================================
outline:
  title_candidates:
    - "Phase-Modulated Compound Sparsity: How Eviction Strategy and Reasoning Phase Interact in Sparse LLM Inference"
    - "Emergent Phase-Strategy Interaction in Compound Sparse LLM Inference"
    - "When Compound Sparsity Bites Back: Phase-Dependent Severity Amplification in Importance-Based Eviction"

  sections:
    - id: abstract
      title: Abstract
      summary: >
        Compound sparsity (head pruning + KV cache eviction) is assumed to degrade uniformly.
        We show the interaction is strategy-dependent and phase-modulated: importance-based eviction
        exhibits 12-75× severity amplification in low-sparsity reasoning phases, while random eviction
        stays flat (~1×). Bootstrap CI (B=10000) confirms significance at all 4 sparsity levels (p<0.0001).
        Cross-model replication on Qwen2.5-7B validates generalizability. We explain this via an
        entropy-discrimination collapse mechanism: head pruning distributes surviving attention,
        destroying importance score discriminability specifically in distributed-attention phases.
      length: 250 words

    - id: introduction
      title: "1. Introduction"
      summary: >
        Motivate compound sparsity as practical deployment need. State gap: prior work (SparK, Ada-KV)
        treats compound interaction as uniformly super-additive. Our finding: the severity is an
        emergent property of the interaction between eviction strategy and reasoning phase.
        Preview crossover phenomenon and mechanism. State contributions.
      length: 1 page
      key_claims:
        - Compound sparsity severity is not uniform — it is strategy-dependent and phase-modulated
        - Importance-based eviction amplifies compound interaction 12-75× in low-sparsity phases
        - Entropy-discrimination collapse explains the phase-strategy interaction

    - id: related_work
      title: "2. Related Work"
